3.core:
A start came and its shape was clear, and you put it down. Not out of failure — it just went quiet. Since then the door you were standing at has closed, but you are still at it, and the energy is going into standing there. What is in your hands now is smaller than what you actually carry. The beginning is yours and it is still unstarted.

So make one full look. Gather the whole of the old start onto one page or table — what it was, what is still tangled in it, what you keep not looking at — and look until there is nothing left unseen. No verdict, no restart required. When nothing is hidden, this ends, and the thing can end with it. Then, and only then, note the piece of it that still wants to be done.
3.sheetLine: You left the start and stayed at the door.

4.tense: The shaping is in your hands now, and your own account says it happened on its own.
4.verb: Starting the thing in its first form and giving it a shape someone else can hold.
4.place: The room where what you already are is becoming visible and nothing is being added to make it true.
4.ask: The thing quietly taking form through you: lay all of it out at once, the way you would spread papers across a table — what you have been doing, and what it adds up to — until you have seen it without adding or taking away.
4.core:
Somewhere in this beginning, the shaping is yours. The order is being kept, the words are being placed, the timing is being held — and the account you carry says it just came together, nothing much to notice. The start is being written. You, asked, would say it wrote itself.

Catch it once. At whatever moment you are quietly doing the shaping, stop long enough to see what you are actually doing — and then keep going. Nothing has to be announced. Seeing the whole of it for one second is enough to put your name back on it, and the work is the same either way; it just stops belonging to a stranger.
4.sheetLine: The plan is being written by your hand. You say it wrote itself.

1.tense: You are at the start of something and can hold its whole shape while you begin.
1.verb: beginning something and giving it a form you can see
1.place: a vantage where the whole shape of a thing is visible at once
1.ask: Pick the smallest buildable job on the list this week and carry it right through to done — a repair, a page, supper for someone else — then let that person share in the finished thing.
1.core:
You know how to begin. Something concrete is here worth giving form to, and you can hold the whole shape of it while you're still at the start — that's rare, and it's what this vantage is for. You don't need to see the finished version to trust the first move.

What's next that's concrete? Choose the smallest job you can actually carry through to done this week — a repair, a sketch, a page, supper for someone else — and take it all the way. Don't narrate it. Let it exist. The finished object will tell you more about what you can build than any plan would. Once you've done it, you'll know where the strength was.
1.sheetLine: You can hold the whole shape while you begin.

2.tense: The beginning hasn't happened yet and you're already bracing for what it will demand.
2.verb: beginning something and giving it a form you can see
2.place: a vantage where the whole shape of a thing is visible at once
2.ask: Give fifteen minutes to a single page about the thing you're bracing for — every part and feeling, all at once, named. No plan, no fix, nothing crossed out.
2.core:
You are holding everything about this beginning that hasn't happened yet, and you're scanning the whole pattern, and you can't find a place to put your hand. The beginning is still ahead. It hasn't been written yet.

You can predict almost anything from the shape of it. That's the vantage working hard, not a flaw. But prediction turns to bracing the same way, and bracing makes the waiting heavier than the thing itself. So take it out of your head: name the whole of it, every part and feeling at once — no plan, no fix, nothing crossed out. The beginning doesn't need to be fully understood before it can be taken up. Bracing and beginning feel similar. They are not the same move.
2.sheetLine: You're already carrying what hasn't started yet.

3.tense: That beginning is already behind you, and you haven't stepped through the door it was supposed to open.
3.verb: beginning something and giving it a form you can see
3.place: a vantage where the whole shape of a thing is visible at once
3.ask: Take the next small step of something you've been avoiding and spread everything it actually involves on paper or the floor, so all of it sits in view together.
3.core:
There's a beginning that already happened and you didn't step into it, and you're still at the door. The shape of it is mostly closed to you. The strength this vantage runs on isn't there right now, and it can't be forced.

Direct sight is the way through, small. Take the next small piece of something you've been avoiding, spread it out so the whole of it sits in view — the actual steps, not the story about them — and look until nothing is missing. Seeing it whole is enough for now. The door stays closed and that's fine. The whole shape can sit where you can look at it.
3.sheetLine: You're still at a door that already closed behind you.

4.tense: You can see whole situations before anyone else does, and you don't count it as yours.
4.verb: beginning something and giving it a form you can see
4.place: a vantage where the whole shape of a thing is visible at once
4.ask: When the whole picture arrives before anyone else's does, put a name on it — 'this is what I see' — before checking whether anyone would agree.
4.core:
You can see the whole shape of something before anyone else at the table has started, and you have a habit of putting the pen down right after. You tell yourself you're keeping your head low. The others just call it quick.

You've been handing your reading off — calling it circumstance or group effort before it has a chance to be yours. Let it be complete once. When the whole picture arrives before anyone else's does, put a name on it before checking whether anyone would agree. What you can see is real and it is yours. Nobody has to sign off on it.
4.sheetLine: You see it before the room does, and you don't take the credit.

1.tense: Right now you are standing at the start of something you mean to build.
1.verb: starting the first piece of what will be built
1.place: at the launch point
1.ask: Pick a concrete thing someone near you needs, do it now, and see it through to done.
1.core:
Right now you are holding the first piece of something you mean to build, and it is doing what a first piece should: it is turning into the rest. When a start lands well, the made thing gets made and the next move is obvious by itself. You are working on one of those and there is no need to look past it.

A concrete hand offered to someone near you, taken all the way to finished in one sitting, keeps the line moving. Not a sweeping gesture — enough to close before the tea goes cold. That is what makes a beginning readable: someone else can see it, and so can you, and neither of you has to call it anything.
1.sheetLine: A finished thing makes the next one obvious.

2.tense: You are pushing for a completion that cannot be imagined from here.
2.verb: starting the first piece of what will be built
2.place: at the launch point
2.ask: Take a page, name every feeling this one has stirred, and leave every one of them standing.
2.core:
You are pushing something toward a finished shape that cannot be imagined from here, and the pushing runs ahead of anything you have. There is nothing to brace against yet — the next step has no picture, and it cannot be forced into one. Hoping harder will not get it.

Before the next move, put every feeling about this onto one page, all of them, none crossed out. It will not fit a theme and it will not be tidy. Stay with the page until the whole of it is legible, and the push will have somewhere to stand. What is actually complete can be measured against it rather than guessed at.
2.sheetLine: You are forcing a shape the thing cannot wear yet.

3.tense: You were standing at the start of something, and the starting has gone quiet.
3.verb: starting the first piece of what will be built
3.place: at the launch point
3.ask: Put all of it out where it can be taken in at once, and stay with it until no piece is left turned away.
3.core:
A first piece of something was there, and it has gone quiet. What you meant to build lives as a heap in a back room — all still sitting, none of it started, and you in front of it half turned away. The pull toward it is still in you. It is not doing anything right now.

Put the pieces where they can be taken in together — no cupboard, no stack, everything in view. Stay with them until no piece is left turned away, and start nothing. What is whole there is already yours to take in; that alone is the first cut of a beginning, and it will not need pushing from you.
3.sheetLine: You want it built, and nothing has been started.

4.tense: The pen is already moving on this building, with your hand not claiming it.
4.verb: starting the first piece of what will be built
4.ask: Look at one finished piece already on the table until you can take it in whole, and take it as yours.
4.core:
The pen is already moving on this building, and you talk about it as if nothing is happening. You are making small finished pieces and calling them luck, or saying anyone would have. The pieces are on the table — the concrete bit is real. The maker part of the work is the part you have not put your name to.

Take one finished thing that is already done, and look at it until you can see all of it at once — what it took, what it's made of, that it stands. No credit to argue for. Holding it whole, with no doorway left to hide behind, is how a beginning gets kept, and you will need it kept for the next one.
4.sheetLine: The building is already underway in your name.
